title: Run Massive-Scale UMAP in Minutes Using Multiple GPUs—Without Losing Accuracy | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA cuML and cuVS 25.06 add multi-GPU support for the expensive all-neighbors kNN graph construction step of UMAP, distributing work across GPUs without all-to-all communication. On the 106M-vector MIRACL dataset, eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs deliver up to 74x speedup over projected CPU runtime, completing 870 GB of vectors in 8 minutes while preserving embedding quality.

insights.claim: NVIDIA cuML multi-GPU UMAP on eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs achieves up to 74x end-to-end speedup over projected CPU runtime on the 106M-vector MIRACL dataset, completing end-to-end processing in just 8 minutes.
insights.speaker: Jinsol Park
insights.so_what: Turning multi-hundred-gigabyte UMAP from days into minutes makes interactive large-scale exploration feasible only on GPU, a concrete workload moat.
insights.quote: On the 106M vector MIRACL dataset, cuML achieves up to 74x end-to-end speedup over the projected CPU runtime.

insights.claim: At full scale the widely used CPU UMAP reference implementation failed to complete because of excessive memory consumption even on a system with 2 TiB of RAM, forcing NVIDIA to project CPU runtimes by extrapolation.
insights.speaker: Jinsol Park
insights.so_what: The CPU path simply cannot run these workloads, so GPU acceleration is not a speedup but an enablement of otherwise impossible analysis.
insights.quote: At full scale, the CPU implementation failed to complete because of excessive memory consumption, even on a system with 2 TiB of RAM.

insights.claim: cuML multi-GPU UMAP shows strong scaling as GPUs increase from one to eight H100s, with performance continuing to improve while preserving comparable embedding quality (trustworthiness) across configurations.
insights.speaker: Jinsol Park
insights.so_what: Near-linear scaling means users buy more speed by adding GPUs, incentivizing larger NVIDIA GPU deployments per workflow.

insights.claim: cuVS 25.06 partitions the dataset into balanced clusters with overlap across nearby clusters, computes local kNN graphs independently per cluster, and merges them into a global all-neighbors graph, distributing work across GPUs without expensive all-to-all communication.
insights.speaker: Jinsol Park
insights.so_what: Avoiding all-to-all communication is what lets the method scale across GPUs where distributed kNN workloads usually stall.
insights.quote: Computing these local kNN graphs independently avoids the need for expensive all-to-all communication that would typically limit scale in distributed all-neighbors kNN workloads.
insights.locator: How does NVIDIA cuML UMAP scale across multiple GPUs?

insights.claim: The construction of an all-neighbors kNN graph, which finds the k-nearest neighbors for every vector, is the critical UMAP step that becomes increasingly expensive as datasets scale to tens or hundreds of millions of vectors.
insights.speaker: Jinsol Park
insights.so_what: Identifies the true bottleneck that the multi-GPU work targets, explaining why prior single-GPU approaches remained limited.

insights.claim: Two hyperparameters govern the tradeoff: knn_n_clusters sets partitioning (memory scales inversely with it) and knn_overlap_factor sets cross-cluster overlap (memory scales proportionally), with knn_overlap_factor=2 a good starting point for quality embeddings.
insights.speaker: Jinsol Park
insights.so_what: Gives practitioners a controllable space-time-quality dial, keeping per-GPU memory constant by scaling both parameters together.
insights.quote: knn_overlap_factor and knn_n_clusters together provide a controllable trade-off between space, time, and quality.
insights.locator: How to configure UMAP for multiple GPUs

insights.claim: The GPU all-neighbors graph preserves neighborhood relationships and produces embeddings with comparable global structure to the CPU reference on the 106M x 2048 MIRACL dataset, maintaining high trustworthiness scores at massive scale.
insights.speaker: Jinsol Park
insights.so_what: Speed without accuracy loss removes the main objection to GPU acceleration, making adoption low-risk for existing UMAP users.
insights.quote: The resulting embeddings show comparable global structure, demonstrating that the GPU all-neighbors graph preserves the neighborhood relationships needed to produce high-quality visualizations even at a massive scale.

insights.claim: All benchmarks ran on an NVIDIA DGX system with eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs and an Intel Xeon 8480CL 224-core CPU with 2 TiB of RAM, using the trustworthiness score (0 to 1) to measure how well local neighborhood structure is preserved.
insights.speaker: Jinsol Park
insights.so_what: The results are anchored to NVIDIA DGX hardware, framing DGX as the reference platform for massive-scale data science.
insights.locator: What is the performance of multi-GPU UMAP

insights.claim: The cuVS all-neighbors API is exposed standalone so a precomputed GPU all-neighbors graph can be fed to UMAP via the precomputed_knn argument, an argument that the CPU UMAP implementation also accepts.
insights.speaker: Jinsol Park
insights.so_what: Interoperable graph handoff lets users accelerate just the expensive step while keeping existing UMAP pipelines, easing incremental adoption of RAPIDS.
insights.locator: How to use multi-GPU UMAP in NVIDIA cuML

insights.claim: The multi-GPU all-neighbors capability ships in NVIDIA cuVS and unlocks UMAP training in cuML at unprecedented scale, making large-scale workflows like topic modeling and single-cell analysis more practical via the RAPIDS stack.
insights.speaker: Jinsol Park
insights.so_what: Extending RAPIDS to previously intractable scales pulls more of the Python data-science ecosystem onto NVIDIA GPUs.
insights.locator: Get started with UMAP using multiple GPUs
